p.src: Now Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie were just about to use their magic to hold the women fast when they suddenly heard the rush of wind and Sha Wujing shouting. They turned in haste and saw that the Tang Monk had vanished. Wukong said, “Who has come and carried Master off?” Sha Wujing replied, “It was a woman. She raised a whirlwind and swept Master away.” At these words Wukong gave a whistle, leapt into the clouds, shaded his eyes with one hand, and looked all around. He saw only a cloud of dust, with the wind rolling through it, receding toward the northwest. He turned back at once and called, “Brothers, mount your clouds quickly and come with me after Master!” Bajie and Sha Wujing promptly fastened the baggage to the horse; then, with a rush, they all sprang into the air.

p.src: The ruler, ministers, and women of Western Liang were so alarmed that they knelt in the dust, saying, “Those are arhats ascending to Heaven in broad daylight. Your Majesty need not be frightened or doubtful. The Tang Emperor’s younger brother is likewise an accomplished Chan monk. Blind though we had eyes, we mistook him for an ordinary man from China and wasted all this anxious scheming. We beg Your Majesty to mount the carriage and return to court.” The queen felt ashamed, and all the officials returned together to the capital. Of them we shall speak no more.

p.src: Meanwhile, the three brothers Sun Wukong, Bajie, and Sha Wujing soared through the air and trod the mist, pursuing the whirlwind without pause. When they reached a lofty mountain ahead, the dust had settled and the wind dispersed, leaving them with no idea which way the fiend had gone. The brothers lowered their clouds, searched for a path, and began looking about. Presently they saw to one side a smooth, gleaming wall of blue stone shaped like a screen. Leading the horse, the three went around the stone screen. Behind it stood a pair of stone doors bearing six great characters: “Pipa Cave, Venomous Foe Mountain.” The witless Bajie stepped forward at once and raised his rake to smash the door. Wukong hurriedly stopped him. “Brother, do not be hasty. We followed the whirlwind here, but only found this door after searching for some time, and we still know nothing of what lies within. If this is not the place, would we not provoke its owner for nothing? You two take the horse back around the stone screen and wait there a while. I shall go in, make inquiries, and learn whether our suspicions are true before we act.” Sha Wujing was delighted to hear this and said, “Good, good, good! Even in roughness there is care; in truth, the more urgent the matter, the more calmly it should be handled.” The two of them led the horse back.

p.src: Wukong squeezed through a crack beside the door and flew beyond the second gateway. In a flower pavilion directly ahead sat a female fiend. Around her stood several young maids in bright embroidered garments, their hair tied in twin knots, all brimming with delight as they discussed something or other. Wukong flew softly up and clung to the latticework of the pavilion to listen. Just then he saw two tousle-haired girls with childish topknots carry up two steaming plates of pastries and say, “Mistress, one plate holds meat buns filled with human flesh, and the other holds vegetarian buns filled with sweet bean paste.” The female fiend laughed. “Girls, help the Tang Emperor’s younger brother out here.” Several of the brightly dressed, embroidered-robed maids went to the rear chamber and helped the Tang Monk out. His face was yellow, his lips pale, and his reddened eyes streamed with tears. From his hiding place Wukong sighed, “Master has been poisoned.”

p.src: The fiend descended from the pavilion, extended ten slender fingers like spring onions, seized the elder, and said, “Set your mind at ease, dear Imperial Brother. Though this is not the palace of the Women’s Kingdom of Western Liang, nor so rich and splendid, it is in truth a peaceful and carefree place, perfectly suited to chanting the Buddha’s name and reading the scriptures. You and I shall become companions in the Way and truly live in harmony for a hundred years.” Tripitaka said nothing. The fiend said, “Do not distress yourself. I know that when you attended the banquet in the Women’s Kingdom, you took neither food nor drink. Here are two plates of food, one with meat and one vegetarian. Take whichever you please to settle your nerves.” Tripitaka pondered silently, “If I refuse to speak or eat, this fiend is not like the queen. The queen was at least human and conducted herself according to propriety; but this creature is a demon spirit. What am I to do if she means to harm me? My three disciples do not know that I am trapped here. If she harms me, would I not lose my life for nothing?” Reasoning thus with himself and finding no other course, he forced himself to take heart and asked, “What is in the meat dish? And what is in the vegetarian one?” The female fiend replied, “The meat buns are filled with human flesh, and the vegetarian buns with sweet bean paste.” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk eats vegetarian food.” The fiend laughed. “Girl, bring hot tea, and let your venerable elder enjoy the vegetarian buns.” One of the girls duly brought a cup of fragrant tea and set it before the elder. The fiend split open a vegetarian bun and handed it to Tripitaka. Tripitaka passed her a meat bun whole and unbroken. The fiend laughed. “Dear Imperial Brother, why did you not split it open for me?” Tripitaka joined his palms. “As a monk, I dare not break open meat.” The female fiend said, “If you monks dare not break meat, why did you drink so deeply from the Child-and-Mother River the other day, yet today are so eager to eat bean-paste filling?” Tripitaka replied, “When the water is high, the boat goes swiftly; when sand engulfs the path, the horse goes slowly.”

p.src: Listening through the lattice as the two traded words, Wukong feared that his master’s true nature might be led astray. Unable to restrain himself, he resumed his own form, drew his iron staff, and shouted, “Insolent beast!” When the female fiend saw him, she spat out a stream of smoky light that shrouded the flower pavilion and ordered, “Girls, take the Imperial Brother away.” Then she seized a three-pronged steel fork, leapt through the pavilion doorway, and cursed, “You wretched, impudent monkey! How dare you sneak into my home and spy upon my beauty? Do not flee! Take a thrust from your old mother!” The Great Sage blocked her weapon with his iron staff, fighting as he retreated, until the two battled their way out of the cave. Bajie and Sha Wujing were waiting before the stone screen. Suddenly seeing the two locked in combat, Bajie hurriedly led over the white horse and said, “Sha Wujing, you just guard the baggage and horse while old Zhu goes to lend a hand in the fight.” The good idiot raised his rake in both hands, rushed forward, and cried, “Elder Brother, stand back! Let me strike down this vile shrew!” Seeing Bajie approach, the fiend employed another trick. With a cry she sent fire from her nostrils and smoke from her mouth, shook her body, and whirled her three-pronged fork as she charged to meet him. No one could tell how many hands the female fiend had as she came tumbling at them in a wild flurry of blows. Wukong and Bajie pressed her from both sides. The fiend said, “Sun Wukong, you truly do not know when to advance or retreat. I know who you are, but you do not know me. Even the Buddha Tathagata in your Thunderclap Monastery is afraid of me. What can you two hairy creatures possibly amount to? Come at me together, and each of you had better watch closely for my blows!” And what a fine battle it was:

p.src: The three fought for a long time without victory or defeat being decided. The female fiend suddenly sprang upward and unleashed her Backward-Horse Venomous Sting, pricking the Great Sage on the scalp before he knew it. Wukong cried, “Agony!” Unable to endure the pain, he abandoned the fight and fled in defeat. Seeing that matters had gone awry, Bajie dragged his rake away and retreated. Having won the battle, the fiend put away her steel fork.

p.src: The Pilgrim clutched his head, his brow furrowed and his face twisted in pain, crying, “Terrible! Terrible!” Bajie came up and asked, “Brother, just when the fight was going so well, why did you suddenly flee, crying out in pain?” Still clutching his head, the Pilgrim could only cry, “It hurts! It hurts! It hurts!” Sha Monk said, “Perhaps your old headache has returned?” The Pilgrim sprang up and said, “No, no!” Bajie said, “Brother, I never saw you wounded. Why, then, does your head hurt?” Groaning, the Pilgrim said, “This is dreadful, truly dreadful. While I was fighting her, she saw that I had broken through the play of her fork. Then she suddenly leapt, and with some weapon I could not identify, stabbed me once on the head. The pain became unbearable, and that is why I retreated defeated.” Bajie laughed. “When all is peaceful, you are forever boasting that your head has been tempered by cultivation. How is it that you could not withstand this one little stab?” “That is precisely the mystery,” said the Pilgrim. Ever since I cultivated myself and attained the Truth, stole and ate the immortal peaches, drank the celestial wine, and swallowed Laozi’s golden elixir, and then raised havoc in Heaven, the Jade Emperor had the Mighty Ghost King and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions drag me to the Palace of the Dipper and the Ox to be executed in every possible way. Those divine generals attacked me with blades, axes, hammers, and swords, with thunderbolts and fire; and when Laozi placed me in the Eight Trigrams Furnace and refined me for forty-nine days, not one of those things did me any harm. Yet today, I know not what weapon that woman used to injure old Sun’s head.” Sha Monk said, “Take your hands away and let me look. Has the skin been broken?” “No, it has not,” said the Pilgrim. Bajie said, “I will go to the Kingdom of Western Liang and fetch a plaster for you.” The Pilgrim said, “It is neither swollen nor broken. How could a plaster be applied?” Bajie laughed. “Brother, I never suffered any illness before or after giving birth, yet you have somehow developed a boil on your forehead!”

p.src: Sha Monk said, “Second Brother, enough of your jokes. Night has now fallen, Elder Brother has injured his head, and we do not even know whether Master is alive or dead. What are we to do?” The Pilgrim grunted, “Master is all right. When I went inside, I changed into a honeybee and flew in, and saw the woman seated in a flower pavilion. Presently two maids brought two plates of steamed buns: one contained meat filling made from human flesh; the other contained sweet bean-paste filling and was vegetarian. Then she had two young girls help Master out to eat one and settle his nerves, saying that she wanted to become some sort of Dao companion to him. At first Master neither answered the woman nor ate a bun. But after hearing her honeyed words and sweet talk, I know not how, he began to speak and said he would eat the vegetarian one. The woman split open a vegetarian bun and handed it to Master. Master handed the woman a whole meat-filled one. The woman asked, ‘Why do you not split it open?’ Master replied, ‘A monk dares not break open meat.’ The woman said, ‘If you will not break open meat, why did you drink your fill beside the Mother-and-Child River the other day, yet today are so fond of sweet bean-paste filling?’ Master did not understand her meaning, and answered with a couplet: ‘When waters rise, the boat speeds on; when sand sinks, the horse goes slow.’ Listening from the lattice, I feared that Master’s nature might be thrown into disorder, so I revealed my true form, drew my cudgel, and struck. She also used her magic, belched out smoke and mist, and cried, ‘Take the imperial brother away!’ Then she swung her steel fork and fought old Sun all the way out of the cave.” Hearing this, Sha Monk bit his finger and said, “Who knows from where that shameless wretch followed us? She knows everything that happened before.”

p.src: Now the female fiend laid aside her ferocity, composed her face anew into a joyous expression, and ordered, “Underlings, bolt both the front and rear gates securely.” She also assigned two guards to keep watch for the Pilgrim and to report at once if they heard the gates move. Then she ordered, “Girls, put the bedchamber neatly in order, light the candles and burn incense, and invite the imperial brother of Tang here, so that I may make love with him.” Thereupon they helped the elder out from the rear. The female fiend displayed every manner of coquettish charm, took hold of the Tang Monk, and said, “As the proverb goes, ‘Gold is not truly precious; a life of ease is worth far more.’ Come, let us play at being husband and wife for a while.” The elder clenched his teeth and uttered not a sound. He wished to refuse to go, but feared that she might take offense and kill him. He therefore had no choice but to follow her trembling into the perfumed chamber. He remained as if witless and mute, never raising his head or lifting his eyes. He did not look at what bed, curtains, chests, or dressing things the room contained. Nor did he heed the female fiend’s amorous enticements in the least. What a fine monk he was! Truly:

p.src: The two of them traded scattered words and broken phrases until deep into the night, but Elder Tang’s mind remained wholly unmoved. The female fiend tugged and pulled at him without letting go, but the master remained sober and steadfast in his refusal. She pestered him until midnight, when at last the fiend lost her temper and cried, “Underlings, bring a rope!” Pitifully, the one she professed to love was trussed with a rope until he resembled a bound macaque. She then ordered him dragged beneath the corridor, blew out the silver lamps, and everyone retired to sleep. Nothing more happened that night.

p.src: The idiot roused his spirits, tightened his black brocade robe, and followed the Pilgrim. Each carrying his weapon, they leapt up the cliff and went straight to the foot of the stone screen. The Pilgrim said, “Wait here. I fear that the monster may have harmed Master during the night. Let me first go inside and investigate. If he was seduced by her, lost his primal yang, and truly ruined his virtue, then we shall all disband; but if his nature remained unconfused and his meditative mind unmoved, then we shall strive our utmost, kill the fiend, rescue Master, and continue westward.” Bajie said, “What a fool you are! As the saying goes, ‘Would anyone give a dried fish to a cat for a pillow?’ Even if it did not go that far, even if it did not, she must at least have scratched him a few times.” The Pilgrim said, “Do not voice wild suspicions. Wait while I go and see.”

p.src: The Great Sage turned behind the stone screen, took leave of Bajie, shook himself, and changed once more into a little honeybee, which flew in through the gate. Inside, he saw two maidservants fast asleep with their heads resting on the watchman's clappers and bells. He went on to inspect the flower pavilion. The fiend and her attendants had been busy half the night and were so weary that none knew dawn had come; every one of them was still asleep. Pilgrim flew around to the rear, where he faintly heard the Tang Monk calling out. He suddenly looked up and saw his master beneath the covered passage, bound hand and foot together like a trussed horse. Pilgrim gently alighted on the Tang Monk's head and called, “Master.” Recognizing his voice, the Tang Monk said, “Wukong, is that you? Quickly, save my life!” Pilgrim said, “And how did last night's happy affair go?” Sanzang gritted his teeth and said, “I would sooner die than consent to such a thing.” Pilgrim said, “Yesterday I saw that she seemed full of tenderness and affection for you. Why has she treated you so harshly today?” Sanzang said, “She pestered me for half the night, but I never loosened my sash or let my body touch the bed. When she saw that I would not yield to her, she bound me here. You must save me, whatever happens, so that we may continue our journey for the scriptures.”

p.src: While master and disciple were conversing, they awakened the fiend. Though she had dealt ruthlessly with him, she still felt a lingering attachment and could not bear to part. As she turned over in her sleep, she caught the words “continue our journey for the scriptures.” At once she rolled out of bed and cried fiercely, “Why go for any scriptures when you could stay and be my good husband?”

p.src: Pilgrim panicked. Abandoning his master, he hastily spread his wings, flew outside, resumed his true form, and called, “Bajie!” The Idiot came around the stone screen and asked, “Did that business come off?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “No, no. Our venerable master refused to yield despite all her fondling, so she grew angry and bound him there. He was just telling me what had happened when the monster woke, and I fled out here in alarm.” Bajie asked, “What did Master say?” Pilgrim said, “He said only that he never loosened his sash and never touched the bed.” Bajie laughed and said, “Good, good, good! He is a true monk after all! Let us go and rescue him.”

p.src: The Idiot was rough and impetuous. Without another word, he raised his rake and brought it down upon the stone gate with all his strength, smashing it into several pieces with a tremendous crash. The maidservants who had been sleeping on the clappers and bells were so frightened that they ran outside the second gate, crying, “Open the gate! The two ugly men from yesterday have smashed down the front entrance!” The female monster had just emerged from her chamber when four or five maidservants rushed in and reported, “Mistress, those two ugly men from yesterday have returned and smashed the front gate to pieces.” On hearing this, the monster hurriedly ordered, “Girls, heat water so that I may wash and dress.” Then she said, “Carry the imperial brother, ropes and all, into the rear chamber and keep him there. I shall go and fight them.”

p.src: What a monster she was! She strode out brandishing her three-pronged fork and cursed, “Impudent ape! Wild boar! What ignorant fools you are! How dare you smash my gate?” Bajie cursed back, “You lecherous slut! You have trapped my master, yet you still dare answer back. You tricked my master into coming here to be your husband. Send him out at once and I will spare you; but if you dare utter even half a ‘no,’ old Zhu will lay into you with his rake and bring down your mountain along with you!” The monster would brook no argument. Bracing herself, she resorted to her former magic: smoke and fire poured from her nose and mouth as she raised her steel fork and thrust at Bajie. Bajie twisted aside to evade the thrust and struck back with his rake; the Great Sage Sun wielded his iron staff and joined forces with him. The monster again displayed her magic. No one could tell how many arms she had as she parried attacks from left and right. After they had exchanged blows for several rounds, some unknown weapon pricked Bajie on the lip. The Idiot dragged away his rake, cupped his mouth, and fled for his life in pain. Pilgrim was somewhat wary of her too. He made a feint with his staff, then yielded the field and fled. Victorious, the monster returned and ordered her underlings to pile up the broken stones and barricade the front gate. Of this no more need be said.

p.src: Now Monk Sha was grazing the horse before the slope when he heard a pig grunting nearby. Looking up suddenly, he saw Bajie approaching, cupping his mouth and groaning. Monk Sha asked, “What happened?” The Idiot groaned, “This is terrible, terrible! It hurts, it hurts, it hurts!” Before he had finished, Pilgrim also arrived and laughed, “You fine Idiot! Yesterday you cursed me for having a boil on my brow, but today you have managed to catch the swollen-mouth plague yourself.” Bajie groaned, “I cannot bear it, I cannot bear it! The pain is dreadful—truly dreadful!”

p.src: As the three of them stood there at a loss, they saw an old woman approaching along the road from the southern mountain, carrying a green bamboo basket in her left hand and returning from gathering vegetables. Monk Sha said, “Elder Brother, that old woman is coming near. Let me ask her for information and find out what sort of monster this is and what weapon she uses to wound people so grievously.” Pilgrim said, “Wait here. Let old Sun go and ask her.” Pilgrim quickly opened his fiery eyes and looked. He saw an auspicious cloud directly above her head and fragrant mist enveloping her on either side. Pilgrim recognized her at once and cried, “Brothers, come and kowtow! That old woman is the Bodhisattva!” Zhu Bajie hurriedly bowed despite his pain, Monk Sha led the horse forward and bent low, and the Great Sage Sun joined his palms and knelt, crying, “Homage to the greatly merciful and greatly compassionate, responsive Guanyin Bodhisattva, savior from suffering and distress!”

p.src: Seeing that they had recognized her halo, the Bodhisattva stepped onto an auspicious cloud, rose into the air, and revealed her true form—the form of the Fish-Basket Guanyin. Pilgrim hastened into the air, bowed, and said, “Bodhisattva, forgive your disciple for failing to welcome you. We were striving to rescue our master and did not know that you had descended. We now face a fiendish trial that we cannot overcome. I earnestly beg you to save us.” The Bodhisattva said, “This fiend is exceedingly formidable. Her three-pronged fork is formed from her two natural pincers. What inflicts such pain when it stings is a hook on her tail, called the Horse-Felling Venom. She is a scorpion spirit in her true form. Formerly, she listened to the Buddha expounding the scriptures at Thunderclap Monastery. When the Tathagata saw her, he unwisely gave her a push with his hand. She turned her stinger upon him and struck the middle finger of his left hand. Even the Tathagata could scarcely endure the pain and at once ordered the Vajra guardians to seize her. But she fled here instead. If you wish to rescue the Tang Monk, you must seek help from another. Even I cannot approach her.” Pilgrim bowed again and said, “Please instruct me, Bodhisattva. Whom should I seek for help? Your disciple will go and invite him at once.” The Bodhisattva said, “Go within the Eastern Heaven Gate to the Palace of Light and appeal to the Sun Rooster of Mao. He alone can subdue her.” Having said this, she transformed into a beam of golden light and returned directly to the Southern Sea.

p.src: Only then did the Great Sage Sun lower his cloud. He said to Bajie and Monk Sha, “Brothers, set your minds at ease. A savior has been found for Master.” Monk Sha asked, “Where is this savior?” Pilgrim said, “The Bodhisattva has just instructed me to summon the Sun Rooster of Mao. Old Sun will go at once.” Cupping his mouth, Bajie groaned, “Brother, ask the star official for some painkilling medicine while you are there.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “No medicine is needed. Just endure the pain through the night as I did yesterday, and you will be well.” Monk Sha said, “Enough chatter. Hurry and go.”

p.src: The splendid Pilgrim hastily mounted his somersault cloud and in an instant reached the Eastern Gate of Heaven. There he suddenly met Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King of Increase, who bowed to him and asked, “Where are you going, Great Sage?” The Pilgrim replied, “While escorting the Tang Monk westward to fetch the scriptures, I encountered a demon who has ensnared him. I am going to the Palace of Light to see the Star Lord of the Pleiades.” Then he encountered the four great marshals Tao, Zhang, Xin, and Deng, who also asked where he was going. The Pilgrim said, “I am seeking the Star Lord of the Pleiades to subdue a demon and rescue my master.” The four marshals said, “This morning the Star Lord received an edict from the Jade Emperor and went to the Star-Watching Terrace to make an inspection.” The Pilgrim asked, “Is that really so?” Celestial Lord Xin replied, “We came out of the Palace of the Dipper and Ox together with him. How would we dare lie?” Celestial Lord Tao said, “He has been gone a long while and may already be on his way back. Great Sage, go first to the Palace of Light; if he has not returned, you may then go to the Star-Watching Terrace.”

p.src: The soldiers at the head of the procession saw the Pilgrim standing outside the Palace of Light. They hurried back to report, “My lord, the Great Sage Sun is here.” The Star Lord gathered in his clouds and mist, straightened his court robes, halted his retinue and divided them to either side. Stepping forward, he bowed and asked, “What brings you here, Great Sage?” The Pilgrim replied, “I have come expressly to trouble you to rescue my master from a calamity.” The Star Lord asked, “What calamity? And where is it?” The Pilgrim replied, “At the Pipa Cave on Poison-Enemy Mountain in the Kingdom of Western Liang.” The Star Lord asked, “What sort of demon inhabits that mountain cave, that you should come to summon this humble divinity?” The Pilgrim said, “The Bodhisattva Guanyin manifested herself just now and said it was a scorpion spirit. She specifically named you, sir, as the only one able to overcome it, so I have come to invite you.” The Star Lord said, “I had intended to return and report to the Jade Emperor, but since you have come here, Great Sage, and I am honored by the Bodhisattva’s recommendation, I fear any delay might hinder matters. I dare not detain you even to offer tea. Let me first go with you to subdue the demon, and afterward I shall return to report on my mission.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Great Sage went out through the Eastern Gate of Heaven with him and headed straight for the Kingdom of Western Liang. When Poison-Enemy Mountain came into sight not far away, the Pilgrim pointed and said, “That is the mountain.” The Star Lord lowered his cloud, and together with the Pilgrim descended beneath the slope before the stone screen. Sha Monk saw them and said, “Second Brother, get up! Elder Brother has brought the Star Lord.” The Idiot, still holding his mouth, said, “Forgive me, forgive me. I am ill and cannot pay my respects.” The Star Lord said, “You are a man of religious cultivation. What illness could you have?” Bajie replied, “This morning, while fighting that demon, she stabbed me in the lip, and it still hurts.” The Star Lord said, “Come here, and I shall treat it for you.” Only then did the Idiot take away his hand. Moaning and groaning, he said, “Please, you must cure it. Once I am well, I will thank you.” The Star Lord ran a hand over his lips and blew a breath upon them; at once they ceased to hurt. Delighted, the Idiot bowed and cried, “Marvelous! Marvelous!” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “May I trouble you, Star Lord, to rub my head as well?” The Star Lord replied, “You have not been poisoned. Why should I rub it?” The Pilgrim said, “I was struck by it yesterday, but after a night had passed, it stopped hurting. It is still somewhat numb and itchy, and I fear it may flare up in cloudy weather. Please treat it too.” The Star Lord duly rubbed his head and blew a breath upon it. The remaining poison was dispelled, leaving neither numbness nor itching. Bajie said fiercely, “Brother, let us go beat that vile slut!” The Star Lord said, “Indeed, indeed. You two call her out, and I shall subdue her.”

p.src: Bajie stepped forward, planted one foot upon the monster’s chest and back, and said, “Accursed beast! You cannot use your horse-felling poison this time.” The monster did not move. The Idiot laid into her with his rake and pounded her into a mass of pulp. The Star Lord gathered his golden radiance once more, mounted a cloud, and departed. The Pilgrim, Bajie, and Sha Monk cupped their hands toward heaven in thanks and said, “We have greatly troubled you. Another day we shall visit your palace to repay the favor.”

u.src: Bajie stepped forward, planted one foot upon the monster’s chest and back, and said, “Accursed beast!
You cannot use your horse-felling poison this time.”
The monster did not move. The Idiot laid into her with his rake and pounded her into a mass of pulp.
The Star Lord gathered his golden radiance once more, mounted a cloud, and departed.
The Pilgrim, Bajie, and Sha Monk cupped their hands toward heaven in thanks and said, “We have greatly troubled you.
Another day we shall visit your palace to repay the favor.”

p.src: When the three had finished giving thanks, they gathered their luggage and horse and all entered the cave. There they saw maidservants young and old kneeling on both sides. They bowed and said, “Grandfathers, we are not evil spirits. We are all women of the Kingdom of Western Liang, abducted here earlier by this demon. Your master is sitting and weeping in the incense chamber at the rear.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim examined them carefully and found that they indeed bore no demonic aura. He went into the rear chamber and called, “Master!” When Tang Monk saw that they had all arrived, he was overjoyed and said, “My worthy disciples, I have caused you much trouble. What became of that woman?” Bajie replied, “That wretch was actually a great female scorpion. Fortunately, the Bodhisattva Guanyin gave us guidance, and Elder Brother went to the celestial palace and invited the Star Lord of the Pleiades to descend and subdue her. Old Hog then raked her into mud. Only after that did we dare venture this deep and see our master’s face again.” Tang Monk thanked them without end. They found some rice and noodles for vegetarian fare, prepared a meal, and ate their fill. They sent the abducted women down the mountain and pointed out the road home. Then they lit a fire and burned the several buildings completely to the ground. They helped Tang Monk onto his horse, found the main road, and continued westward. Just so:
